nameStory: Cherry-plum gets its name from being a fascinating hybrid between cherries and plums, combining characteristics of both fruits. This botanical mashup creates fruits that look like small plums but often taste more like cherries, earning it this perfectly descriptive double name.
description: Cherry-plum is a small ornamental tree or large shrub that typically grows 15-25 feet tall. It's originally from Asia but has been planted as a landscape tree throughout New England for its showy spring flowers and colorful foliage. The tree produces small, round fruits that range from yellow to deep red or purple, and many cultivars have striking purple or bronze-colored leaves that make them popular in gardens and parks.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves with finely toothed edges, often deep purple or bronze-red in ornamental varieties, though some are green. Feel smooth on top with a slight shine, and they're arranged alternately along the branches.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Delicate white or pale pink flowers with five rounded petals appear in early spring before or with the leaves. They have a sweet, light fragrance and cluster densely along the branches, creating a showy display.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small, round drupes about the size of large cherries, ranging from yellow to red to deep purple. The flesh is sweet but often somewhat bland, and each contains a single hard pit like a cherry.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth, gray-brown bark on young trees that develops shallow furrows with age. Often has small horizontal lenticels (breathing pores) that feel slightly raised to the touch.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a rounded crown with somewhat upright branching when young, becoming more spreading with age. Often has multiple trunks or branches low to the ground, especially when used as an ornamental shrub.

habitat: Cherry-plum is primarily found in cultivated settings throughout New England - in parks, residential landscapes, and occasionally escaped along roadsides or forest edges. It prefers well-drained soils and full sun to partial shade, thriving in disturbed areas where it can sometimes naturalize.

seasonality.spring: Produces masses of white or pink flowers in early spring, usually April, creating a spectacular but brief display. New leaves emerge bronze or purple in colored varieties, bright green in others.
seasonality.summer: Full foliage shows off the distinctive leaf color - deep purple, bronze, or green depending on variety. Small fruits ripen from green to their final colors of yellow, red, or purple by midsummer.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellow or orange before dropping, though purple-leafed varieties often retain their color. Fruits may persist briefly but are usually gone by early fall.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the tree's rounded structure and smooth bark with small lenticels. Flower buds are visible as small, pointed structures along the twigs.

funFact: Cherry-plum trees are actually one of the parent species of many domestic plums you buy at the grocery store, making this ornamental tree a direct ancestor of fruits that end up in your kitchen!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other ornamental Prunus trees like flowering cherry or regular plum trees. Look for the distinctive purple or bronze foliage in ornamental varieties - most other flowering trees in this family have green leaves. The small, round fruits help distinguish it from cherries, which are usually more heart-shaped.
contextualKnowledge: Cherry-plum is often called 'myrobalan plum' in horticultural circles, and many of the trees you see are actually grafting rootstock that has grown up and flowered. This means some 'wild' cherry-plums are actually the hardy root portion of grafted fruit trees that outlived their grafted tops.
compareHints: Unlike native cherries which have clusters of flowers, cherry-plum flowers appear more individually along branches. It differs from American plum by its typically purple foliage and smaller, rounder fruits. Beach plum stays much smaller and grows in coastal areas, while cherry-plum is inland and can reach true tree size.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's wild cherries, black cherry stands out by growing into a large tree with distinctively scaly bark.
Among New England's native cherries, chokecherry is distinguished by its upright flower clusters and tendency to form thickets.
Unlike its Prunus relatives, beach plum stays low and shrubby rather than growing into trees like black cherry or chokecherry.
Fire cherry differs from its cousin black cherry by being much smaller in stature and having narrower leaves, plus its flowers bloom in flat clusters rather than long drooping racemes.
Wild cherry stands out from its Prunus relatives by its distinctive peeling bark and drooping flower clusters.
Among New England's wild cherries, sand cherry is unique for its low, spreading habit – all the others (black cherry, chokecherry, fire cherry) grow as upright trees or tall shrubs.
Unlike tall cherries like black cherry or chokecherry that grow as trees, Susquehanna Sandcherry stays low and shrubby.
Among its Prunus relatives, Canada plum stands out with its distinctively dark bark - much darker than American plum or any of the cherries.
Peach trees are smaller and shorter-lived than most of their Prunus relatives in New England.
Unlike cherries in the same genus, American plum has larger, rounder fruits that don't grow in hanging clusters, and the fruits have the characteristic plum 'seam' running along one side.
Compared to native American plums, domestic plums produce larger, less tart fruits and grow into taller trees.
Unlike its common Prunus relatives like chokecherry and black cherry, blackthorn is heavily armed with long, sharp thorns and stays shrub-sized rather than becoming a tree.
Among its Prunus relatives, sour cherry is distinguished by its small size and weeping growth habit - most other cherries in New England grow much taller and more upright.
Bird cherry stands out from other New England Prunus species by its long, drooping flower clusters that appear after leaf-out, unlike our native cherries which bloom before or with emerging leaves.

Unlike our native black cherry which has white flowers in long clusters and darker, scaly bark, North Japanese hill cherry has pink flowers in shorter, drooping clusters and smooth, glossy reddish bark.
Unlike native New England Prunus species like wild cherry or chokecherry which grow as large trees, flowering almond stays shrub-sized and is clearly ornamental.
Among the Prunus species in New England, Nanking Cherry is unique for its consistently shrubby growth habit and fuzzy leaves.
